implementation_notes: Python makes a god object unusually easy to write and unusually hard to see, because privacy is by convention: a module whose `import *`-reachable names include every function in the subsystem is a god object with no class at all, and nothing stops any other module from calling any of them. The Named Conference style and the `from module import name` discipline are the practical mitigations; typed, narrow protocols are the structural one. When the god object is a real class, `self.<field>` accessed from outside the class (or from tests) is the reach you are looking for. `pylint`'s too-many-instance-attributes / too-many-public-methods and a quick `grep -c 'self\.'` per class are the cheap detectors; the decomposition is the same everywhere: a dataclass per cohesive group of fields, functions taking those dataclasses, and the god object's methods becoming functions.
idiom_name: module as god object (module globals are the state)
code_sketch:
# app.py: module-as-god-object
db = connect()

def login(u): ...
def sync(): ...
def render(): ...

# split: one cohesive module per responsibility
# invoicing.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Invoice:
    lines: list[Line]
    total: Money = field(init=False)
    def calculate(self) -> Money: ...
pitfalls: `from x import *` silently re-exports the god object into every importing module, so the reach is invisible in any single file.
`__all__` only restricts `import *`; attribute access `mod.thing` still works for anyone.
A module-level singleton is not reset by `importlib.reload` in the way people expect — the old module object survives in every importer's namespace.
